extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and researchers (number theory, real analysis, geometry, combinatorics/graph theory)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of procedural requirements, definitions, proof techniques, and estimation methods used in evaluating or producing rigorous mathematical arguments across topics: evaluation of ζ(2) (Euler's series), double-integral substitutions, Dehn invariants and equidecomposability, Sylvester–Gallai and related incidence/graph decomposition theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Substitution Formula (double integrals)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute a double integral ∫∫_S f(x,y) dx dy we may perform a substitution of variables x = x(u,v), y = y(u,v) if the correspondence of (u,v) ∈ T to (x,y) ∈ S is bijective and continuously differentiable. Then I equals ∫∫_T f(x(u,v),y(u,v)) |det J| du dv, where det J is the Jacobi determinant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required conditions: bijectivity and continuous differentiability of the mapping; replace dx dy by |Jacobian| du dv. Use this to simplify integrands or domains; remember to account for orientation/absolute value of determinant and possible symmetry factors when restricting to halves of domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating double integrals by geometric-series expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand an integrand like 1/(1-xy) as a geometric series, decompose summands as products, then integrate termwise over a product domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method can turn a difficult integral into a double sum that separates into product integrals. Ensure uniform convergence on the domain so termwise integration is justified. Used here to derive the ζ(2) value from a double integral; also shows finiteness despite a pole on the boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate transformation: rotate/scale and account for Jacobian
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply an affine or linear coordinate change (e.g. rotate the unit square by 45° and shrink) to transform the domain; when changing variables replace dx dy by |det J| du dv to compensate area change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the transformation yields symmetry, exploit it to reduce the computation (e.g. integrate over half the domain and multiply). Keep track of constant multiplicative factors arising from the Jacobian (example: factor 2 when areas are reduced by 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design substitutions so Jacobian cancels the integrand (Beukers–Calabi–Kolk style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an explicit bijective trig substitution mapping the unit square to a triangle (u>0, v>0, u+v<π/2) so that the Jacobian simplifies the integrand to a constant, reducing the integral to the area of the image domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal: find x(u,v), y(u,v) that invert explicitly and whose Jacobian algebraically cancels denominators in the integrand. Check bijectivity and compute the determinant explicitly; when successful the integral may reduce to a simple geometric quantity (area/volume). This approach generalizes to higher even zeta values via higher-dimensional analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting a series into even and odd parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose a series into its even-term subseries and odd-term subseries to relate the total sum to simpler sums (e.g., separate ζ(2) into contributions from even and odd n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to find relations between known sums and target sums; combine with integral representations to exploit symmetry. Keep track of multiplicative factors when relating even-indexed sums to the full sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summation via trigonometric-polynomial roots (cotangent identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive identities for sums like Σ cot^2(θ_r) by taking the imaginary part of (cos x + i sin x)^n, evaluating at roots, dividing by sin x, and observing that cot^2 of certain angles are roots of a polynomial; then compare coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method outline: write sin(nx) as polynomial·sin x, evaluate at specific x where sin(nx)=0 to get roots, form polynomial with roots cot^2(·), then use Vieta/coefficient comparison to obtain sums of roots. Carefully justify algebraic manipulations and the degree/number of roots used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequalities sin x < x < tan x to bound trigonometric series
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 0 < sin x < x < tan x for 0<x<π/2 to derive 0 < cot x < 1/x < csc x and obtain bounds for terms involving cot and csc, enabling comparison and convergence estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these pointwise inequalities to each term and then sum; combine with identities (from cot/csc relations) to obtain two-sided bounds on sums or to show convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing a series with an integral for tail estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the remainder of a convergent positive-term series by comparing it to an appropriate integral (∑_{n>m} f(n) ≈ ∫_{m}^∞ f(t) dt) and refine using convexity if available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard tool for bounding series tails and obtaining explicit error bounds (upper/lower). If f is decreasing/convex, use integral test inequalities (∫_{m+1}^∞ ≤ tail ≤ ∫_{m}^∞) or improved convexity-based bounds for tighter estimates. Example: error in partial sums of ∑1/n^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic expansion of partial sums involves Bernoulli numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The error term in partial sums of classical series (e.g. partial sums of ζ(2)) admits an asymptotic expansion whose coefficients are Bernoulli numbers; this expansion explains subtle digit-pattern phenomena in computed partial sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extreme numerical accuracy is studied, examine the asymptotic expansion of the remainder; consult references (e.g. Borwein, Borwein & Dilcher) for full expansions and proofs. Use these expansions to predict and interpret surprising numerical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Dehn invariant D_f(P)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a 3-dimensional polyhedron P let A_P be the set of dihedral angles together with π. Given a finite set M ⊇ A_P and any Q-linear function f: V(M) → Q with f(π)=0, define the Dehn invariant D_f(P) := ∑_{edges e} length(e)·f(angle(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction requires choosing a finite M containing all dihedral angles of the polyhedron and a Q-linear functional f vanishing on π (and hence on 2π, etc.). The Dehn invariant depends on f; examples: for a cube D_f(C)=0 for any such f because of rational relations. Use D_f to detect non-equidecomposability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity of Dehn invariant under decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polyhedron P is decomposed into finitely many polyhedral pieces P1,...,Pk and all dihedral angles of the pieces are contained in M, then for every Q-linear f: V(M)→Q the Dehn invariants add up: D_f(P) = ∑_{i} D_f(P_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: assign to each edge-part a 'mass' length·f(angle); interior edges cancel because the angles sum to π or 2π so f(π)=f(2π)=0. This additivity is the key tool for comparing Dehn invariants of equidecomposable (or equicomplementable) polyhedra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q-linear extension lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite subsets M ⊂ M' ⊂ R, any Q-linear function f: V(M) → Q can be extended to a Q-linear f': V(M') → Q so that f'|_{V(M)} = f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend a basis of V(M) to a basis of V(M') and define f' arbitrarily on the new basis vectors (subject to linearity). This allows choosing f on a small set of angles and extending it to any larger finite angle set encountered in a decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dehn–Hadwiger criterion for non-equicomplementability
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists a Q-linear f: V(M)→Q with f(π)=0 such that D_f(P) ≠ D_f(Q), then polyhedra P and Q are not equicomplementable (and hence not equidecomposable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the additivity of D_f under decomposition: if P and Q were equicomplementable one would get equality of D_f values after matching congruent pieces; thus a witnessing functional f proving inequality obstructs equicomplementability. This is the main tool to resolve Hilbert's third problem examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing functionals f using irrational ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a finite angle set M whose Q-vector space V(M) has dimension >1 (e.g. because some angle ratios are irrational). Define f by setting f(π):=0 and assigning a nonzero rational value to one angle from a Q-basis, yielding D_f nonzero for some polyhedra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice: identify an angle α whose ratio with π is irrational (per results from earlier chapters), take M = {α, π}, then define f(α)=1, f(π)=0. Compute D_f for candidate polyhedra to obtain contradictions with cubes whose Dehn invariant vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: equidecomposable and equicomplementable polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: Two polyhedra P,Q are equidecomposable if they can be decomposed into finite sets {P_i} and {Q_i} with Pi congruent to Qi for all i. They are equicomplementable if there exist finite polyhedral additions {P'_j},{Q'_j} such that P ∪ ⋃P'_j and Q ∪ ⋃Q'_j are equidecomposable (interiors disjoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking decomposability or complementability, allow reflections (congruences can include orientation reversal). Equicomplementability is weaker than equidecomposability and requires checking possible finite augmentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylvester–Gallai extremal proof technique
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove existence of a line through exactly two points in a non-collinear finite point set, choose a pair (P,ℓ) with P not on ℓ minimizing the distance from P to ℓ; show ℓ must contain exactly two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extremal/choice method exploits minimality to derive contradictions if ℓ had three or more points. The proof uses metric/order axioms of the real plane (though variants use only order axioms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–de Bruijn lower bound on number of lines
rubrics_metrics.description: For n>3 points in the plane not all collinear, the set C of lines through at least two points contains at least n lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction: remove one point lying on a line containing exactly two points (by Sylvester–Gallai); either the remaining points are non-collinear and apply induction, or they are collinear and count the pencil of lines. Use Sylvester–Gallai as base of the inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motzkin/Conway incidence-system bound (m>n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be an n-element set and A1,...,Am proper subsets such that every pair of elements of X is contained in precisely one Ai. Then m>n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proof templates: (a) combinatorial counting using r_x (# of sets containing x) and double-counting inequalities; (b) linear-algebraic: incidence matrix B (n×m) has B B^T positive definite hence rank(B) ≥ n, forcing m>n. Use whichever approach is more convenient for the instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham–Pollak theorem and linear-algebraic proof (Tverberg)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the complete graph K_n is decomposed into m complete bipartite subgraphs H_1,...,H_m, then m ≥ n-1. Tverberg's proof assigns variables x_i to vertices and derives a linear system showing that m < n-1 would give a nontrivial solution leading to contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up equations expressing that each pair of distinct vertices i≠j contributes exactly once across the bipartite subgraphs; if there are fewer equations than unknowns (m<n-1) obtain a nontrivial kernel vector whose properties contradict the decomposition. The known proofs are linear-algebraic; no purely combinatorial proof is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposing K_n into stars as an upper-bound construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple decomposition of the complete graph K_n into n-1 complete bipartite graphs is obtained by taking stars K_{1,n-1}, K_{1,n-2}, ..., K_{1,1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows the trivial upper bound m ≤ n-1; combining with Graham–Pollak gives the exact minimum m = n-1 for star-based decompositions. Use this construction as a baseline or to motivate tighter lower bounds.
